events.title: South Africans vote in a new democracy
events.description: The first national democratic election open to all races marks a major change.

events.title: Windows 95 launches
events.description: Microsoft introduces its new operating system with a Start menu and taskbar.

events.title: Pathfinder lands on Mars
events.description: The mission reaches the surface carrying the small Sojourner rover.

what_happened_next.text:
Microsoft grew to more than fourteen times its starting value, while Intel grew to more than seven times. Both far outpaced the US share basket in this window. Disney also more than doubled. These striking gains do not make every technology stock a sure winner. The prices still moved unevenly, and the result depends on this particular five-year window.

The next five years included South Africa’s first national democratic election open to all races, the launch of Windows 95 and the arrival of the Pathfinder mission on Mars. Windows 95 was directly connected to Microsoft’s business. Even so, a successful product launch alone could not tell an investor the size or timing of a stock gain.

An amount growing to fourteen times its starting value is very different from gaining fourteen percent. This was an unusually large result. A broad basket could grow substantially and still trail these two companies. Owning the basket meant sharing in many businesses rather than depending on just one. Neither choice came with its future result attached.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: The Fed was beginning to raise short-term rates, entertainment companies were combining, and computer makers were selling new products.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: The chosen technology shares gained much more than the broad basket. The basket put less money in those winners, but it also relied on more than one business succeeding.
reflection.what_faded_away: A small initial interest-rate increase did not tell you the final ranking. An Olympic victory and a takeover contest were interesting news, but not a map of future returns.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: Nobody knew these exact gains in advance. Today’s familiarity with Microsoft and Intel can make their earlier risks easier to overlook.

hot_stock_outcomes.text: Windows 95 arrived in August 1995, making home computers easier to use. Office 97 and Windows NT also brought in business customers. By the year ending June 1998, Microsoft earned $4.49 billion on $14.48 billion of sales. June 1998 also brought Windows 98. Growing software sales and profits help explain the stock’s powerful rise.

More people buying computers meant more demand for Intel’s chips. Pentium II arrived in 1997, and Intel expanded into cheaper PCs with Celeron in 1998. Annual sales reached $26.3 billion in 1998. Profit slipped that year as prices and costs squeezed earnings, but the much larger chip business helps explain why the shares finished so far ahead.

The Lion King became a huge movie hit in 1994. Disney then completed its purchase of Capital Cities/ABC in early 1996, adding a large television business. Animal Kingdom and the Disney Magic cruise ship opened for customers in 1998. These gave Disney more ways to earn money from entertainment, helping the company grow beyond its films and older parks.
